host: x86-64 Intel Core Ultra 9 285H, P-core (cpu2), taskset-pinned, rdtscp; see results/host.json
summary: Three deployed libraries' Minerva (ECDSA nonce bit-length) fixes, checked against the corpus's at-the-site constant-time requirement. Each fix fails or holds for a distinct, measured reason, and a leak/clean analyser cannot tell them apart. The MatrixSSL case is a shipped, default-enabled constant-time fix that does not close the leak through the vendor's latest open release.

libgcrypt.fix_location: internal ECDSA signing (_gcry_dsa_modify_k) plus a clamp in the secure-memory scalar-multiplication path
libgcrypt.outcome: fix moved UPSTREAM of the primitive
libgcrypt.detail: The public gcry_mpi_ec_mul an analyser can be pointed at leaks the scalar bit-length in BOTH versions (short scalar ~half the cycles of a full one, either way); only the internal secure-nonce signing path is fixed. A primitive-level tool sees no change across the patch. Recovery-certified via real signing (pairs/libgcrypt-minerva, ORC-1/2 pass).
libgcrypt.site_closure_basis: Definition 4, tab:closure row 2: the secret-dependent construct is present at the primitive s an analyser drives and absent along the deployed signing path s'; decided by the two-sided recovery, not by a timing test at s.

wolfssl.fix_location: wolfcrypt/src/ecc.c ecc_mulmod timing-resistant path (ECC_TIMING_RESISTANT): loop bound changed from get_digit_count(k) to get_digit_count(modulus), leading-zero fast path removed
wolfssl.outcome: NOT DECIDABLE BY THIS INSTRUMENT. Corrected 2026-08-25: an earlier revision graded this 'fix HOLDS'. It does not follow from what we measured. Our own two-sided oracle requires the recovery to SUCCEED on the vulnerable arm and fail on the patched one; here the lattice fails on both, at 6,000 and at 50,000 signatures. A recovery that cannot demonstrate the bug cannot certify the fix, so this pair does not meet the corpus's admission rule and its verdict is withdrawn rather than kept at reduced confidence.
wolfssl.detail: The vulnerable timing-resistant path already balanced leading-zero bits with dummy add/double operations, so the deployed 4.0.0 residual is only 0.029% (256-bit vs <=254-bit nonces, medians over 6000 signatures, reconstructed from the known key). dudect reads BOTH arms clean at one-bit granularity (vuln tau 0.0164, patched 0.0076, both within the null band), and the Minerva lattice attack fails on both at 6k and 50k signatures. The non-timing-resistant default path is byte-identical between the two releases, so building with defaults would not discriminate the arms at all.
wolfssl.residual_method: 0.029% is the difference in MEDIAN whole-signature time between 256-bit and <=254-bit nonces over 6000 signatures, nonces reconstructed from the known signing key. It is a whole-signature figure, not a scalar-multiplication one; the dudect numbers quoted for wolfSSL are the separate at-the-site measurement.
wolfssl.decision_rule_basis: DECIDED UNDER THE RETIRED TAU BAND, and this is the one case in the study that is not decided by the permutation rule the paper now uses. The wolfSSL arms were measured before that rule replaced the band, their raw dudect samples are not committed under results/raw/, and there is no pairs/wolfssl* tree, so the case cannot be re-decided without rebuilding 4.0.0 and 4.1.0 and re-acquiring. The reading is unlikely to change: both arms sat far inside the band (0.0164 and 0.0076) rather than near it, and the lattice recovered from neither at 6,000 or 50,000 signatures, which is a decision that does not depend on the statistical rule at all. But 'neither arm rejects its own permutation null' would be a claim about a test we did not run, so the paper does not make it.
wolfssl.why_this_is_a_finding_not_only_a_retract: The deployed 4.0.0 arm was ALREADY balanced with dummy operations to a 0.03% residual before the patch under test was written, so what our instrument would have had to detect is a leak the vendor had largely closed one release earlier. That is a boundary of the method rather than a gap in this case: fix verification as defined here needs an exploitable vulnerable arm, and a leak already too small to exploit falls outside its reach. Naming that boundary is more useful than grading the case, because it says which remediations this method can and cannot audit.
wolfssl.taxonomy_note: This case no longer populates the 'attenuated' cell of the fix taxonomy. The attenuation it exhibits is the pre-fix 4.0.0 build's own dummy-operation balancing, which predates the 4.1.0 patch under test, so crediting it to that patch would attribute to the fix an effect present before it.
wolfssl.site_closure_basis: Outside the domain of Definition 3: the oracle demonstrates the bug on neither arm, and the only timing readings were taken under the retired band on uncommitted samples, so no delta or MDE is printed for it.

matrixssl.fix_location: crypto/pubkey/ecc_math.c eccMulmodCt, added in 4.3.0 explicitly 'in response to the Minerva attack' (release notes) and enabled by default (cryptoApi.h: USE_CONSTANT_TIME_ECC_MULMOD). The fix adds dummy point operations to the leading-zero (mode 0) branch, which in 4.2.1 was a bare 'continue'.
matrixssl.outcome: fix INCOMPLETE; residual persists through the latest open release
matrixssl.detail: CORRECTED 2026-08-25. An earlier revision attributed the residual to eccMulmodCt still setting its loop bound from get_digit_count(k) (ecc_math.c:206, unchanged 4.2.1 through 4.6.0). That attribution was ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE for the measurement that produced the number: get_digit_count counts DIGITS, DIGIT_BIT is 64 on this x86-64 build, and a 255-bit and a 256-bit scalar both occupy 4 digits, so both classes run the identical 256 loop iterations. A four-design decomposition on the fixed 4.3.0 build localises the real mechanism:

matrixssl.dudect_note: CORRECTED 2026-08-26 after the rebuild. Every figure in the *_RETIRED blocks of this record came from a harness that passed a zeroed curve `a` coefficient where the library passes NULL, so it timed scalar multiplication on a different curve at 3.46x the cost of the deployed call (3.42x the library's own key generation, the harness_overstatement_factor in results/matrixssl_containment.json). Those blocks are kept renamed so the change is visible; the figures in force are measurements_full_report.designs, re-acquired three times per design from a retained build (results/matrixssl_repeats.json). The one-leading-zero class difference is 1,575 ticks on 4-2-1 (between-acquisition range 155) and 1,093 ticks on 4-3-0 (range 116). No attenuation ratio is quoted between them, because the two releases are separately built arms and nothing here bounds between-build variation, which is the paper's rule; the fivefold figure an earlier revision reported is withdrawn for that reason and for the harness error, and is not replaced by another ratio. The latest open release is indistinguishable from the first fixed one, and where the nonce is short by a whole digit the fixed builds are about twice as leaky as the pre-fix build. See results/matrixssl_containment.json and results/matrixssl_repeats.json.
matrixssl.exploitability: LEAK-PRESENCE CERTIFIED, NOT RECOVERED BY THE PUBLISHED ATTACK. Decided 2026-08-27 by nine timing-ordered lattice attempts on the fixed build (results/matrixssl_recovery.json, generator bin/matrixssl_recovery.py, attempt records under results/raw/matrixssl/lattice/): the vendored upstream Minerva attack, which sorts signatures by their own timing and hands the fastest to the lattice, over budgets of 25,000, 50,000 and 100,000 signatures and lattice dimensions 90, 110 and 130, recovered the key in none. The selection is not what stops it: on traces acquired with nothing else running on the host, at 50,000 and 100,000 signatures, the fastest 90 are 5.6% contaminated by full-length nonces at AUC 0.61 and 0.62 (results/exploit_budget_matrixssl_50000.json, results/exploit_budget_matrixssl_100000.json), close to the 3.3% at which libgcrypt's pre-fix leak yields. What stops it is the per-signature bound: the attack's rank model credits its top-ranked signatures with a multi-bit bias and builds a basis on 814 to 1,361 bits of assumed information against a 256-bit key, while the deployed fix leaves one bit of nonce length. That is a bounded observation about this attack and this residual, not about the number of signatures; an attack fitted to a one-bit bias needs a different lattice, which this artifact does not build. HISTORY. The field read 'LEAK-PRESENCE CERTIFIED, RECOVERY PENDING' from 2026-08-25 until this decision, and that revision's own correction stands: Corrected 2026-08-25; an earlier revision of this field claimed the leak 'feeds a recoverable hidden-number-problem' and blamed the failure to recover on a fast host. Both are withdrawn. The lattice run behind the first claim was fed nonces already labelled with the private key, which assumes the selection an attacker must derive from timing. The host excuse does not survive measurement either: on the same host and the same estimator, on the committed 25,000-signature 4-3-0 trace and key, the AUC between signing time and nonce shortness is 0.6256 here against 0.8018 for libgcrypt (n=6,000), which does yield, and the fastest 90 signatures are 28.9% contaminated by full-length nonces here against 3.3% there (results/exploit_budget_matrixssl.json, results/exploit_budget.json). The limit is how much information the leak carries, not how noisy the host is. The reading: leak-presence certified, recovery pending. RETIRED 2026-08-27: an earlier revision of this field also read 'the AUC is 0.6335 (n=250,000; 0.6338 at n=5,999, so it is not a trace-length artifact)', 'at a matched budget the fastest 90 are 44.4% contaminated' and 'raising this arm's budget forty-fold improves it only to 26.7%'. Both endpoints of that sweep came from the 250,000-signature trace that results/exploit_budget.json's _correction identifies as the mislabelled 4.2.1 pre-fix build, so the matched-budget comparison, the budget sweep and the not-a-trace-length-artifact inference are withdrawn, not merely uncommitted, as budget_reading_RETIRED_note in that record says.

matrixssl.mechanism: The residual is the leading-zero phase, not the loop bound. For a scalar with one extra leading zero, exactly one loop iteration is converted from the real path to the mode-0 dummy path, and the two are balanced by OPERATION COUNT but not by COST: the dummy double is out-of-place (P != R) so eccProjectiveDblPoint executes three pstm_copy calls the in-place real double skips, and the dummy operands are the fixed (P, 2P) rather than evolving ladder state, so the ~15 value-dependent conditional add/sub branches inside each point operation and the conditional final subtract in pstm_montgomery_reduce behave differently. The effect is close to linear in the number of leading zeros: on the fixed build the class difference is 1,146 ticks at one leading zero on the committed dump (1,093 averaged over the three acquisitions in results/matrixssl_repeats.json, range 116) and 71,994 at sixty-three (measurements_full_report.designs), where |t| saturates above 200 on every release; at one leading zero |t| reads between 17 and 23 across the three releases, so the saturation belongs to the sixty-three-zero design alone and not to the 255-v-256 design that shares its digit count. The get_digit_count(k) loop bound is a genuine secret-dependent bound, but for 256-bit nonces it only changes when the nonce is short by a whole 64-bit digit, probability 2^-64, so it is not the leak a real nonce distribution exercises.
matrixssl.general_claim: Control-flow balancing by operation count does not deliver constant time on a variable-time arithmetic substrate. pstm's multiply and reduce loop over the operands' used digits and branch on magnitude, so a dummy operation that matches the real one instruction for instruction can still differ in cost. Balancing must be of cost, not of count.

An earlier revision of this note went on to say that what it lacks is enough separation for a rank-based selection to deliver a clean short-nonce set; that was a property of the committed 25,000-signature trace's acquisition, not of the residual, since the quiet-host traces select at 5.6% contamination (corrected 2026-08-27). What the residual lacks is depth: one bit per signature where the published attack's model assumes many.

cross_cutting: The corpus's reproduction pairs detect because they are amplified (40x per-bit work); these deployed leaks in shipped configurations are 0.03% to sub-percent, at or below a fast host's timing floor. That gap between a tool benchmark and a real attacker is itself a measured result, and it is why recovery certification, not a tool verdict, is the label.

taxonomy.note: A fix-outcome taxonomy, so a case study of three becomes a classification other cases can be added to. The classes are defined by what the patched build does to the leak at the declared site, which is what the at-the-site check measures.

classes.removed: the secret-dependent operation is gone from the patched build at the site
classes.relocated: the leak is closed, but the fix sits outside the primitive an analyser is pointed at, so the primitive is unchanged across the patch
classes.attenuated: the mechanism remains and the residual is reduced below what an attack can use at a stated budget and host
classes.reshaped: the mechanism changes channel (for example a branch becomes an address) rather than being closed
classes.incomplete: the mechanism remains and the residual is still measurable at the site

taxonomy.unpopulated_note: Neither of the three cases removes the mechanism outright or moves it to a different channel, so those two classes are named and empty rather than dropped: the taxonomy states what a larger survey would have to fill.

survey_triage.method: Triage-first: for each candidate the fix commit or release is located and the pre/post scalar-multiplication path is READ, and the fix is classified into the taxonomy from source alone, before any build. This predicted MatrixSSL's loud unbalanced leak and wolfSSL's balanced one correctly, and it costs minutes where a build-and-acquire cycle costs hours. Only candidates whose diff predicts a discriminating pair are then built. Candidates NOT built are recorded here with the reason, so the survey's coverage is legible rather than implied.

Crypto++ CVE-2019-14318 (8.2.0->8.3.0).triage: History.txt for 8.3.0 records 'fix elliptic curve timing leaks (CVE-2019-14318)'. The fix replaces branches on the point identity with arithmetic masking, six sites commented 'Gyrations attempt to maintain constant-timeness', of the form P.x * IdentityToInteger(!P.identity). This is a FOURTH strategy: neither relocation, nor loop-bound correction, nor dummy operations, but branch-free selection by multiplication. It is a promising pair because the masks are Integer multiplies on a bignum layer that is itself variable time in operand size, which is the same substrate trap the MatrixSSL case identifies.
Crypto++ CVE-2019-14318 (8.2.0->8.3.0).not_built_reason: Crypto++ is C++, and none of the corpus's pinned offline toolchain images carries a C++ compiler; building it would require adding and digest-pinning a new build cell. The pair is therefore triaged from source and classified, but not measured, and it is recorded as such rather than being claimed or dropped.

SunEC (Minerva advisory).triage: not pursued: the affected code is Java/JNI inside the JDK, so a dudect harness would measure the JIT and the JNI boundary as much as the primitive, and the corpus has no build cell for it

survey_triage.coverage_statement: Five candidates triaged. Three (libgcrypt, wolfSSL, MatrixSSL) are built and measured end to end. Crypto++ is classified from source as a fourth fix strategy but not measured, because the pinned toolchain has no C++ compiler. SunEC is out of reach for this corpus. The survey therefore reports three measured outcomes and one source-level classification, and says which is which.
